name: Abiraterone acetate

lead: Abiraterone acetate is a prescription oral drug for advanced prostate cancer. It comes up in androgen-focused discussion as a theoretical route to protecting scalp hair or skin, because it sharply lowers testosterone and DHT.

It inhibits the enzyme CYP17A1 in the testes, adrenal glands and tumours, cutting production of testosterone and related androgens; it is given with prednisone to offset the resulting hormone imbalance. No study among the sources reviewed has tested it for hair loss, acne or other appearance outcomes.

paras: It is not used for appearance. It is taken by mouth with prednisone under oncology supervision for prostate cancer.
Labelled risks include high blood pressure, low potassium, fluid retention, adrenal insufficiency, liver toxicity and fetal harm. It is prescription-only and used under oncology supervision.

angle.text: Abiraterone lowers the body's androgen production, so in theory less DHT reaches the follicle and hair thins more slowly. It is a prostate-cancer drug, not used for appearance, and no hair or skin studies were found.

lead: Abiraterone acetate (brand names Zytiga and Yonsa) is an oral prodrug converted in the body to abiraterone, an inhibitor of the enzyme CYP17A1, which lowers production of androgens including testosterone and DHT. It is approved for advanced prostate cancer, given with prednisone, and is a prescription cancer drug rather than a cosmetic or dermatological product.[1][2][3]

It is included here because it is discussed in connection with anti-androgen approaches to hair. No published study among the sources reviewed has tested abiraterone for hair loss, acne or any other appearance outcome, so its effect on appearance in people is untested.
Its labelled risks include mineralocorticoid excess effects (hypertension, low potassium, fluid retention), adrenal insufficiency and liver toxicity, and its label states it can cause fetal harm.
infobox: Institute of Cancer Research (London); marketed by Janssen (J&J)

paras: No approved or studied appearance use was found in the sources reviewed. Wikipedia and the US label describe only oncology indications.[1][3]

Abiraterone acetate with prednisone is indicated for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and metastatic high-risk castration-sensitive prostate cancer.[1][3] A fixed-dose combination with the PARP inhibitor niraparib is approved for BRCA-mutated metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer.[2] Randomized trials reported improved overall survival in patients who had received chemotherapy, in those who had not, and in castration-sensitive disease.[4][5][6][7] Guidelines and reviews place it among standard treatments.[8][9]

The US label warns of mineralocorticoid excess (hypertension, hypokalemia, fluid retention), adrenocortical insufficiency and hepatotoxicity, which is why it is given with a corticosteroid and monitored.[3] Wikipedia lists urinary tract infection, low potassium, high blood pressure, diarrhea and swelling as very common effects, and fractures, arrhythmia and raised liver enzymes as common.[1] The label states that the drug can cause fetal harm and that safety and efficacy have not been established in females.[3]

Abiraterone inhibits 17 alpha-hydroxylase/C17,20-lyase, an enzyme expressed in the testes, adrenal glands and prostate tumours, blocking androgen synthesis at several sites.[1][3] Wikipedia also notes weak androgen receptor antagonism and that a 5-alpha-reduced metabolite can act as an agonist.[1] Food increases absorption, so the label directs it be taken on an empty stomach.[1][3] Resistance mechanisms such as the AR-V7 splice variant have been studied.[10]

Researchers at the Institute of Cancer Research in London developed abiraterone in the early 1990s, using ketoconazole as a model; Johnson & Johnson acquired it in 2009, the FDA approved it for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer in April 2011, and approval for castration-sensitive disease followed in 2018.[1]
It is prescription-only in most markets, with generics in the US and India.[1] No community discussion sources were reviewed for this entry.

No studies found in hair loss, acne or other appearance indications. Prostate cancer evidence is extensive: the COU-AA-301 trial reported improved survival after chemotherapy, and later trials reported benefit in chemotherapy-naive and hormone-sensitive disease.[4][5][6][7] Registered trials include formulation, food-effect and adaptive-dosing studies.[11][12][13]

timeline.event: Developed at the Institute of Cancer Research, London.[1]
FDA approval for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer; NEJM trial published.[1][4]
Approval for metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer.[1]
